title: Chartstopper: August 21, 2026
author: Michael Normyle
description: The bond market was the big story this week.
content: This Week The bond market was the big story this week. Long-term Treasury yields have increased in recent months, as 30-year Treasury yields recently hit their high since 2007 , facing pressure from a growing debt load (which hit $40 trillion this week), higher inflation (which we’ll get to), and competition from artificial intelligence hyperscaler bond issuance (boosting investment grade-issuance 36% year-on-year). With yields rising, Treasury Secretary Bessent announced the Treasury will “at least double” its buybacks of long-term (10- to 30-year) Treasuries to $4+ billion from September to November (these buybacks provide liquidity by buying older Treasuries). While this initially led to a drop in long-term bond yields, it’s since reversed, seemingly upon the realization that a few extra billion dollars in buybacks does little in the face of ongoing $2 trillion deficits . In terms of inflation, U.S. oil prices are up about 5% this week as there’s no end in sight for the Iran conflict. Notably, the 60-day Memorandum of Understanding expired this week without extension or even ongoing talks . Instead, Iran seized a United Arab Emirates-linked oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, there were reports Iran’s military is taking a “ fully offensive ” posture as it prepares to a return to war, and President Trump called for “unprecedented” “ economic warfare ” against Iran. Relatedly, in Walmart’s (WMT) earnings this week (beat), the company noted that “higher fuel prices” are causing “some incremental pressure on the consumer .” For the week, the Nasdaq-100® is down 2%, while 10-year Treasury yields are up a few basis points to over 4.7%.

title: Biweekly Investment Insights: AI resurgence propels equities as breadth builds
author: Yanni Angelakos
description: AI-driven earnings and broader EPS growth continue to support equities and market breadth. Softer Fed rate hike expectations are boosting risk assets, even as global bond yields remain near multi-decade highs. While markets may be volatile ahead of U.S. midterm elections, history suggests gains often follow.
content: Yanni Angelakos, Head of Investment Insights, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms Mike Cho, CFA, Senior Research Analyst, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms Tony Kristic, Senior Research Analyst, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Strong earnings push equities to new highs amidst higher rates AI theme continues to underpin equities & earnings, broader EPS growth rates support widening market breadth Softening Fed rate hike expectations have also helped risk assets while global bond yields hover near multi-decade highs Markets historically choppy heading into U.S. November midterm elections, then advance over ensuing months Although the focus is the impact of AI on the U.S. economy and markets, the AI theme is, of course, a global phenomenon. Per our Biweekly Chart in Focus, if looking at Taiwanese exports as a proxy for global AI and technology demand, though annual growth has slowed it remains at a very healthy 39.2% on a YoY basis as of July. Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor YoY returns similarly remain at elevated levels despite having slowed as momentum cooled. From a bottom-up perspective, Q2 earnings season helped allay AI spending concerns in the near-term. However, just as importantly, earnings helped to underpin a broadening of equity returns as U.S. equities hit new highs—the median Russell 3000 EPS growth rate is 15% in Q2 YoY, the highest since Q3 2021. Also helping risk assets over the past two weeks at a macro level were softer July U.S. CPI and PPI reports which scaled back the market pricing of Federal Reserve rate hikes. As of August 17th, there is an 89% chance of a 25 basis point hike by year’s end versus at least one 25 bp hike priced in only a week earlier. While a near-term relief for markets, investors are still contending with multi-year highs in U.S. Treasury yields as the 10-year is at 4.70% and global government bond yields also remain elevated. As the markets move past Q2 earnings, summer winds down, and the calendar turns to September, based on history, we suspect that the market narrative will turn to the U.S. midterm elections in early November. Historically, per Goldman Sachs, market volatility ramps up heading into midterm elections. Yet, these elections tend to be more noise than anything as the S&P 500 typically averages a total return of 14.1% over the six months following midterm elections, since 1970, according to BlackRock. Biweekly Chart in Focus: Taiwanese exports, Nasdaq-100 Index® (Nasdaq-100®), PHLX Semiconductor™ Index YoY% have cooled but still at elevated levels Source: Bloomberg. As of August 14, 2026. Details A strong Q2 2026 earnings season winds down With only about 13% of S&P 500 market cap left to report over the last two weeks of Q2 earnings season (~8% of this being NVDA), around 90% of reporting S&P 500 companies have beaten EPS estimates, per Bloomberg. Focusing on the megacap tech space, which has helped the latest rebound in U.S. equities (Nasdaq-100 is +11% from its July 29 th lows), 89% of Nasdaq-100 companies that have reported as of August 14 th have beaten EPS estimates. The Nasdaq-100 blended (actuals + estimates) EPS growth rate now stands at approximately 76%—significantly higher than the consensus growth forecast of 29.2%. As discussed in our prior piece , while this is skewed by significant contributions from Amazon and Google due to unrealized gains in equity stakes, these are nevertheless very strong earnings trends. Stepping back, the growth rate of the median stock’s EPS in the Russell 3000 Index is 15% YoY—its highest rate since Q3 2021 which benefited from Covid-19-time frame comparisons (Figure 1). Figure 1: Russell 3000 median stock EPS YoY growth Sources: Morgan Stanley, FactSet This widening of EPS growth breadth supports the broadening of U.S. equity returns on a YTD basis (Figure 2) while also keeping equity valuations in check relative to their 10-year averages compared with the middle of 2025 (Figure 3). Figure 2: Thematic 2026 YTD U.S. equity returns Source: Bloomberg. As of August 14, 2026. Figure 3: Global equity next 12-month P/Es relative to 10-year averages Source: Bloomberg. As of August 17, 2026. Softer U.S. inflation trends yet central bank rate expectations and government 10-year yields remain elevated Softer Tier 1 U.S. economic data—July NFPs and retail sales—coupled with cooler-than-expected inflation—July CPI (core inflation was up just 2.5% year-over-year in July, the slowest since 2021) and PPI—caused markets to largely price out a September Fed rate hike. The latest data also brought down expectations for the next several Fed meetings (Figure 4). In the very near-term, the markets will be parsing global central bankers’ signaling at the upcoming Jackson Hole Symposium on August 27 th to 29 th . Figure 4: Number of 25 bp rate hikes or cuts priced in by market for major central banks Source: Bloomberg However, Treasury yields have also remained elevated as U.S. inflation remains a source of concern for the Fed (Figure 5) with oil prices hovering around $80/bbl for WTI crude since late July, Fed policy uncertainties lingering (as we showed in the decomposition of the YTD change in Treasury 10-year yields in our prior piece ), and U.S. government debt levels to climb leading to widening fiscal deficits (Figure 6). This, of course, is not only a U.S. dynamic as global bond yields are at multi-year highs (Figure 7). While market pricing of Fed rate hikes has softened, as Figure 4 also shows, the market pricing of ECB and BoJ’s rates trajectory is higher relative to the Fed as they battle inflation, energy supply shocks (more so than the U.S. which is an energy exporter), and fiscal concerns. Figure 5: U.S. inflation measures have moderated, though remain sticky Source: Bloomberg Figure 6: U.S. federal spending & revenues (% of nominal GDP) Source: Office of Management and Budget, Congressional Budget Office, Peter G. Peterson Foundation Figure 7: Global government 10-year debt yields remain elevated Source: Bloomberg Historical U.S. midterm election trends As recent U.S. elections cycles have shown, predicting outcomes can be very difficult and, though informative, polling can prove to be unreliable. What can be useful for investors is looking at history as a gauge of market reactions leading into and following midterm elections in early November. While historical averages cannot be relied upon as forecasts, Figure 8 below shows that equity volatility usually increases heading into midterm elections but then tends to fade. Figure 9 shows the total return for U.S. equities before and after midterm elections since 1970. The interesting part from Figure 9 is that S&P 500 total returns were 16.1% on average over the six months following mid-term elections in which the President’s party either gains or keeps control of both chambers of Congress. However, when the governing party has a “trifecta” and subsequently loses control of at least one of the chambers of Congress during the midterms, forward 6-month returns were almost 6% lower (10.4%). The takeaway from these charts for investors? If history is any guide, pre-midterm election volatility does not necessarily portend poor forward equity returns and timing the markets is difficult, particularly around what can be unpredictable macro-oriented events. Figure 8: Equity volatility tends to rise headed into midterm elections Source: Goldman Sachs Figure 9: U.S. equities under different midterm election scenarios Source: BlackRock. Notes: “Lost Control” defined as scenarios in which one party was controlling the presidency and both chambers of Congress heading into midterms, then lost control of at least one of them. title: What is the Nasdaq-100? A Guide to One of the World's Most-Watched Indexes
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: At its core, the Nasdaq-100 tracks 100 of the largest non-financial Nasdaq-listed companies, as measured by the total market value of those companies’ outstanding shares.
content: The Nasdaq-100® (NDX®) is a globally recognized index of 100 of the most innovative large cap companies listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market®. Widely used as a benchmark for the technology sector as well as US large cap growth, it's one of the most tracked indexes in the world from an investable product standpoint, with more than $1.7 trillion of exposure linked to it globally as of June 30, 2026. Here's what you need to know. Quick Facts: Inception Date January 31, 1985 Number of Components 100 Weighting Method Modified market capitalization Rebalance Schedule Quarterly Reconstitution Schedule Annual (December) Top Sectors Technology, Consumer Discretionary, Healthcare Financial companies included? No Index Ticker Symbol NDX How the Nasdaq-100 Works At its core, the Nasdaq-100 tracks 100 of the largest non-financial Nasdaq-listed companies, as measured by the total market value of those companies’ outstanding shares. The index uses a modified market capitalization weighting method, which means bigger companies have more influence on the index's movements, but with guardrails in place to prevent any single company from dominating the whole index. This distinguishes it from a pure market-cap-weighted index and helps limit concentration among its top holdings. While the Nasdaq-100 has a longstanding reputation as a "tech-heavy index," its reach goes well beyond Silicon Valley. The Nasdaq-100 is home to companies that have reshaped how we live, work, shop, and connect. The index spans multiple sectors, centering on: Technology — software, semiconductors, hardware Consumer Discretionary — e-commerce, retail, media, entertainment, travel & leisure Healthcare — biotech, medical devices, pharmaceuticals Consumer Staples , Industrials , and Telecommunications Basic Materials, Energy, Utilities, Real Estate (minimal exposure) It's also worth distinguishing the Nasdaq-100 from the Nasdaq Composite® . The Composite includes every company listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market — more than 3,000 securities spanning all sizes and sectors — whereas the Nasdaq-100 is far more selective, tracking only the 100 largest non-financial companies on the exchange. And while many of those components are US-headquartered, the Nasdaq-100 is explicitly not limited to American companies. The index is open to any company listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market — regardless of where that company is based — so it includes globally recognized companies headquartered outside the United States. That international dimension is part of what makes the Nasdaq-100 a global innovation benchmark, not just an American one. Nasdaq-100 vs. S&P 500: Key Differences The Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500 are often mentioned in the same breath, but they're measuring different segments of the market. Here's how they compare: Nasdaq-100 S&P 500 Number of Companies 100 ~500 Exchange Requirement Nasdaq-listed only Any major U.S. exchange Financial Sector Included? No Yes Performance Profile Growth/Innovation-driven Broad U.S. market Sector Concentration New economy focus More balanced The S&P 500 is designed to represent the broad U.S. economy — 500 companies across all sectors, from banks to oil producers to tech giants. By contract, the Nasdaq-100, which trades under the ticker symbol NDX, by contrast, is explicitly focused on non-financial companies at the forefront of global innovation. If the S&P 500 is a snapshot of the economy, the Nasdaq-100 is more of a portrait of where innovation is happening. According to Nasdaq Global Indexes, Bloomberg, and Factset , as of year-end 2025, Nasdaq-100 companies represented slightly more than half of the total market capitalization of the S&P 500, with the average NDX company size approximately three times as large. How a Company Gets Added to the Nasdaq-100 There are specific eligibility requirements a company must meet to be included in the Nasdaq-100. To be considered for inclusion, a company must: Be listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market® or Nasdaq Global Market® tiers Be classified as a non-financial company (banks, insurance companies, and other financial firms including REITs are excluded) Meet minimum average daily trading volume requirements to ensure liquidity Have been listed on Nasdaq for a minimum seasoning period before becoming eligible The index is reconstituted annually each December, when Nasdaq reviews the full list and makes any additions or removals based on updated rankings. In addition, the index is rebalanced quarterly to keep the weighting methodology in check and ensure no single company grows disproportionately large relative to the others. Outside these scheduled events, special rebalances may occasionally take place to manage index concentration, while fast-entry rules enable intra-quarter additions for the very largest companies that conduct their IPOs or switch their listings to Nasdaq, subject to conditions. Top Sectors and Holdings The current Nasdaq-100 components reflect the index's growth-oriented DNA. Technology consistently represents the largest share of the index by weight, followed by Consumer Discretionary and Healthcare. The top holdings by weight typically include companies like Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Tesla, Meta Platforms, and Broadcom — joined by names such as Walmart and Costco. These are some of the largest and most widely held names in global equity markets, and they collectively represent a significant portion of the index's total weight, although they are limited by weight caps applied at the quarterly rebalances and the annual reconstitution. The full list of companies that comprise the Nasdaq-100, in order of their weight in the index, can be found on Nasdaq's website. How to Invest in the Nasdaq-100 Investors can't buy the Nasdaq-100 directly because it is an index, not a security, but there are several practical ways to gain exposure to it. The most popular approach is through exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The Invesco QQQ Trust ETF ( QQQ ) historically tracked the Nasdaq-100's performance, but BlackRock and State Street launched similar funds that also track the index, in July and June of 2026, respectively. Other ETF options exist as well, including leveraged and inverse variants for more sophisticated investors. Mutual funds that track the index are another option, typically accessible through retirement accounts and brokerage platforms. For a full overview of available investment vehicles, visit the Nasdaq-100 Ways to Invest page. Why the Nasdaq-100 Matters Over the long run, the Nasdaq-100 has historically delivered substantial outperformance compared to broader market benchmarks — a reflection of its concentration in high-growth sectors. On a trailing 10-year basis as of December 31, 2025, the Nasdaq-100 has generated total returns of approximately 500% vs. the S&P 500's approximately 300%. Investors can explore historical Nasdaq-100 performance data directly from Nasdaq. That said, higher growth potential also comes with higher volatility. Because the index is concentrated in a smaller set of companies and sectors, it can swing more dramatically than the broader market during periods of economic uncertainty or sector-specific headwinds. For investors, it's both a feature and a risk factor worth understanding. Learn more about the Nasdaq-100® (NDX®). Nasdaq® is a registered trademark of Nasdaq, Inc. title: What Is Nasdaq TotalView? Key Features and Benefits
author: Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms
description: Nasdaq TotalView shows complete order book depth with full liquidity and orders at all prices . Learn how serious traders can use the depth of data for better execution.
content: Key Takeaways Nasdaq TotalView gives traders full depth-of-book visibility, showing every order at every price level instead of only the top levels available through standard Level 1 or Level 2 data. The platform helps active traders and institutions assess liquidity, monitor market participant behavior, and make more informed execution decisions in real time. TotalView’s order-level data, MPID attribution, and ITCH protocol support advanced strategies like order flow analysis, liquidity tracking, and algorithmic trading. NOII adds visibility into opening and closing auction imbalances, helping traders evaluate potential price movement during key market events. Traders can access Nasdaq TotalView through direct feeds, APIs, broker partnerships, or market data vendors depending on their technical needs and trading setup. Professional traders need market visibility to compete. Nasdaq™ TotalView shows you the entire order book for stocks trading on Nasdaq, NYSE, and regional exchanges instead of just the top few price levels that basic data feeds display. You see every order and overall market participant behavior in real time. The average trading volume for US equities hit 12.2 billion shares in 2024, up 10.2% from 2023. Higher volume and fragmented liquidity across venues make complete order book visibility indispensable for optimal execution. Level 2 data shows around 5% of available liquidity, while Nasdaq TotalView shows you the complete book. This level of insight is invaluable when you're planning large executions or trying to identify real support and resistance levels. Global spending on financial market data reached $44.3 billion in 2024, which tells you just how seriously professional traders take data quality. Nasdaq TotalView provides the order book transparency that active traders, institutional investors, and algorithmic systems need to compete.

title: Private Markets Data Expansion: What LPs and GPs Need to Know
author: Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms
description: Private market AUM now exceeds $20 trillion, but data infrastructure hasn't kept pace. Learn how institutional allocators can close the gap with modern technology.
content: Key Takeaways Private market assets under management have grown to more than $20 trillion across all capital structures , making data infrastructure a strategic priority. Manual data extraction and fragmented reporting systems can make meaningful performance benchmarking near-impossible for institutional allocators. Evolving regulatory disclosure frameworks may increase operational reporting demands that can be difficult to address efficiently through highly manual processes. Cloud-native platforms and API-driven integration enable institutional allocators to consolidate fund-level data from multiple sources into a single, searchable environment. Firms that treat data infrastructure as a strategic asset rather than a back-office function may be better positioned to benchmark performance, satisfy regulatory obligations, and make better investment decisions. While private markets represent a significant opportunity for institutional allocators, they also come with complexity and challenges. Assets under management across all private markets capital structures have grown to more than $20 trillion , but the infrastructure supporting it is not keeping pace. As they were built for smaller, simpler allocations, the operational systems used to collect, normalize, and analyze data from private markets remain mostly manual. Many organizations managing multi-billion-dollar alternative portfolios still rely on quarterly PDFs, fragmented GP portals, and spreadsheets. This has led to a widening gap between the scale of opportunities and the information available to act on them. What allocators now need is a framework to close this gap, with supporting technology and implementation steps that investment committees can take.

title: Beyond Earth: The Rise of a Commercial Space Economy
author: Salvatore Bruno, CETF®
description: Explore the rise of the commercial space economy, from satellite communications and AI-enabled data platforms to space infrastructure, and how the Nasdaq-100® provides exposure to this long-term growth theme.
content: Salvatore Bruno, CETF®, Senior Director, Head of Americas Nasdaq Index Insights Sanjana Prabhakar, Senior Specialist, Nasdaq Index Insights Key Takeaways The space economy is entering a multi-decade, infrastructure-led investment cycle, transitioning from government-led to commercially driven markets. Industry growth is supported by a combination of declining launch costs, increased commercial participation, and expanding application areas , though monetization remains uneven across segments. Advances in AI and data processing capabilities are beginning to play a more important role , enabling the extraction of value from large volumes of satellite-generated data across multiple end markets. Government spending and geopolitical considerations continue to provide a structural demand base , particularly in areas such as secure communications, defense, and surveillance infrastructure. While longer-duration opportunities—including space exploration, human spaceflight, and resource extraction— offer potential for future growth, they remain at an early stage and are subject to technological, regulatory, and economic uncertainties. The Nasdaq-100 provides exposure to the space economy through companies that supply the semiconductors, cloud infrastructure, AI capabilities, communications technologies, and data platforms that increasingly underpin space-based applications. Within the Nasdaq-100, participation in the space economy is distributed across multiple layers of the value chain. Rocket Lab may be viewed as the "picks-and-shovels" layer of the space economy , supplying critical infrastructure for launch, satellite deployment, and in-orbit operations. Qualcomm may be viewed as the enabling technology layer , helping connect satellites, devices, and networks through advanced communications hardware and standards development. Industry size is projected to expand from ~$630B (2023) to ~$1.8T by 2035 (~9% CAGR) , outpacing global GDP growth 1 . The space economy and its fundamental underpinnings Investor enthusiasm for the space economy has reached a cyclical high, catalyzed by SpaceX’s IPO at a valuation of over $1.75 trillion—one of the largest public offerings in history 2 . SpaceX marked its debut in the Nasdaq-100® through a “fast entry” rule that allows massive IPOs that meet certain criteria to be eligible to enter the index after 15 trading days. As of July 16, 2026, it ranks as the 8th largest company in the Nasdaq-100 by market cap at $1.8 trillion, slotting in between Broadcom and Meta. However, the company’s index weight is tied to its $106 billion float-adjusted market cap, not its $1.8 trillion headline number. At $106 billion float-adjusted, SpaceX ranks far lower in the NDX® weight hierarchy, comparable in float-adjusted terms to names like Palo Alto Networks, ranking just outside the 20 th largest index weights. SpaceX has officially launched more satellites into orbit than all other companies, governments, and organizations combined in the entire history of spaceflight. It achieved its unprecedented lead by rapidly building and deploying the Starlink mega-constellation. It has launched a cumulative total of 15,262 satellites, recently crossing the threshold to surpass the 15,138 satellites launched by every other entity in human history combined (since 1957). While the rest of the world's total represents nearly seven decades of spaceflight, SpaceX accomplished the majority of its massive deployment in just the last six years 3 . Despite the surge in interest from investors, the space economy remains in the early stages of a multi-decade infrastructure build-out, with capital increasingly directed toward foundational layers such as launch, satellite constellations, and orbital services. The sector’s momentum has been reflected in public equities, with shares of commercial space companies—including Nasdaq-listed Rocket Lab and AST SpaceMobile—delivering outsized gains over the past year. At the same time, comparisons to prior speculative cycles have emerged, underscoring rising valuation risk as capital runs ahead of realized earnings. Structurally, the industry is undergoing a transition analogous to the commercialization of the internet in the 1990s—shifting from a government funded endeavor to a commercial market. This evolution is expanding the addressable opportunity set beyond traditional aerospace into a broad range of applications, spanning launch services, satellite infrastructure, connectivity, Earth observation, defense, and emerging areas such as in-space manufacturing and resource utilization. From a sizing perspective, the global space economy generated approximately $630 billion in revenue in 2023 and is projected to reach $1.8 trillion by 2035, implying roughly 9% annualized growth—well above expected global GDP growth 4 . The investment case is often associated with a convergence of structural demand (government mandates, defense modernization), cost deflation (reusable launch), and expanding commercial applications — with the SpaceX IPO serving as a potential near-term catalyst for the broader sector. Near-term revenue is concentrated in scalable, commercially viable segments , particularly satellite connectivity, positioning/navigation/timing (PNT), and Earth observation, which are driving the majority of current industry growth. Cost declines—driven by reusable launch technologies—are lowering potential barriers to entry , accelerating private-sector participation and increasing deployment activity across the value chain. AI integration is emerging as a critical monetization layer , transforming satellite infrastructure into data-driven platforms and enabling new service-based revenue models. Geopolitical dynamics and defense spending are reinforcing demand , particularly for sovereign communication systems, tracking capabilities, and space-based infrastructure. Longer-duration opportunities—including human spaceflight, in-space manufacturing, and resource utilization—offer significant optionality , but remain early-stage with execution, regulatory, and economic uncertainties. Within the Nasdaq-100, participation in the space economy is distributed across multiple layers of the value chain. While companies like Rocket Lab (a recent NDX addition) represent direct infrastructure exposure, others such as Qualcomm provide enabling technologies—particularly in satellite communications—underscoring the index’s indirect but meaningful exposure to the theme. Qualcomm's space economy participation is primarily centered on enabling satellite-to-smartphone connectivity (D2D), automotive satellite integration, and positioning its chipsets as the underlying silicon for next-generation satellite communication standards. However, these efforts remain a relatively modest component of the company’s broader diversified strategy. Innovations like the Snapdragon X105 5G Modem-RF support both narrowband (messaging) and broadband satellite connectivity without replacing the device 5 . In parallel, Qualcomm has pursued targeted partnerships to advance satellite-enabled use cases. The company has worked alongside Ericsson and Thales Alenia Space to successfully test 5G satellite calls, demonstrating the viability of integrating low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite channels with terrestrial core networks 6 . From an intellectual property perspective, Qualcomm’s positioning is particularly notable. The company has filed roughly 1/6th of all patents within spacecraft and satellite-related technologies in the past few years, per Nasdaq’s analysis of IFI CLAIMS data—underscoring its role in shaping the standards layer of the emerging space communications ecosystem. Rocket Lab positions itself as a fully integrated space company, offering launch services, spacecraft design, component manufacturing, and on-orbit management — making space access more efficient and affordable. The company manufactures spacecraft components, solar arrays, and flight software, and has even acquired robotics leaders like Motiv Space Systems to build Mars-proven technology 7 . It is expanding into medium-lift capacity with their carbon-composite Neutron rocket, which is built for constellation deployments and exploration missions 8 . It is manufacturing 18 satellites for the U.S. Space Development Agency's (SDA) Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture (PWSA) Tracking Layer Tranche 3 program, bringing cumulative SDA awards to over $1.3 billion 9 . Satellite Technology: Unlocking Trillion-Dollar Addressable Markets The investment case for the space economy is increasingly anchored in the rise of satellite communications, positioning/navigation/timing (PNT), and Earth observation as core growth engines, enabling global connectivity and entirely new business models across industries. As satellite technology matures and integrates more deeply with digital systems, it is potentially unlocking trillion-dollar addressable markets. This momentum is reinforced by a surge of deployment activity, with nearly 43,000 satellites forecast to launch over the next decade, representing a total market value of ~$655 billion, with an average of 3,700 launches per year driven primarily by four commercial next-generation satellite orbit (NGSO) mega-constellations 10 . This shift is further amplified by geopolitical dynamics, which are driving sustained demand for sovereign, secure communication infrastructure. Layered on top of these trends is the integration of AI with satellite infrastructure, enabling global, real-time connectivity. Looking ahead, advancements in launch capabilities such as SpaceX’s planned deployment of larger Starlink satellites using its Starship rocket, are expected to further expand constellation capacity. There are ~30,000+ tracked objects in Earth orbit, of which roughly half are active satellites (~16,000), leaving a substantial share as non-functional debris. Collisions between defunct satellites and debris can generate thousands of new high-velocity fragments, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of fragmentation. In a worst-case scenario—often referred to as the Kessler Syndrome—this cascade effect could render entire orbital zones increasingly hazardous or even unusable 11 . As the industry evolves, the market is bifurcating between small, mass-market constellations and large, specialized platforms, with the latter capturing a larger share of industry value. While established aerospace companies and government agencies remain significant players, new entrants such as SpaceX and Blue Origin are reshaping competitive dynamics and traditional business models. At the same time, advanced AI/ML capabilities are expected to be an important near-term driver for converting massive satellite constellation data volumes into near-instantaneous, actionable insights for agriculture, finance, forestry, and government. As data becomes the primary asset, military satellite programs are evolving from asset ownership toward subscription-based data and services models [12] .Ultimately, satellite technology is evolving from a capacity-driven infrastructure buildout into a data-centric ecosystem, where long-term value is determined by the ability to monetize information rather than simply deploy assets in orbit. Satellite Technology: From Infrastructure Buildout to Data Monetization Space Exploration: Catalyst for Dual-Use Technology Space exploration missions have historically been a powerful catalyst for dual-use technology, with advances in propulsion, materials science, robotics, AI navigation, and life support systems translating into broad commercial applications 13 . In this context, the U.S. is increasingly relying on private sector innovation to reduce mission costs, with dual-use technology becoming central for both defense and civilian exploration missions 14 . Recent progress in propulsion technologies, particularly nuclear thermal propulsion (NTP) and solar electric propulsion (SEP), are dramatically cutting travel times to Mars and the outer planets 15 . NASA's Artemis program remains the cornerstone of U.S. lunar ambitions, targeting a sustained human presence on the Moon as a stepping stone to Mars — anchoring long-duration commercial contracts for landers, rovers, power systems, and habitats 16 . SpaceX's Starship — described as the most powerful rocket ever built — is the critical vehicle for both lunar and Mars missions, with upgraded Starlink satellite deployments planned for mid-2027 as an early commercial use case 17 . However, the investment profile of space exploration remains structurally complex. A significant share of exploration revenue is tied to U.S. federal appropriations, which are subject to political and fiscal pressures 18 . While emerging areas such as space tourism, in-space resource extraction, and space-based energy generation offer potentially transformative upside, they remain longer-dated opportunities with considerable execution risk. 19 Deep Space: The Technology Flywheel Behind Space Exploration Commercial Space Travel: Ambitions Continue to Advance The commercial space travel investment case appears compelling on a long-duration horizon — anchored by cost deflation, infrastructure buildout, and landmark IPO catalysts. Early commercial activity is beginning to take shape. Virgin Galactic is targeting the launch of its commercial spaceflight operations in 2026, initially focused on research payloads and private astronaut missions 20 . At the same time, commercial space launches have grown from 11 in 2016 to 157 in 2024, underscoring the impact of reusable rocket technologies in lowering the cost of access to space 21 . Ambitions for deep-space travel continue to advance. SpaceX has announced its first human spaceflight mission to Mars, a two-year Starship mission that will conduct a Mars fly-by, marking a concrete step toward interplanetary commercial travel 22 . Vast and Axiom Space, both developing commercial successors to the International Space Station, are expanding into Europe as NASA signals it may no longer fund development of multiple future stations in Earth's orbit. This shift is creating an opportunity for private operators to capture a larger share of orbital infrastructure and services 23 . Capital formation across the ecosystem is beginning to reflect this transition. Recent investments—including a $100 million commitment to Gemini Space Station —underscore growing private-sector interest in commercial orbital platforms and the broader low Earth orbit (LEO) economy 24 . At the same time, the commercial potential of human spaceflight and on-orbit servicing remains in an early stage of development 25 . Progress will depend on continued advancements in cost, cadence, and reliability of human-rated launch systems , alongside the buildout of supporting infrastructure. Commercial Space Travel: Compelling on a Long-Duration Horizon Space Mining: Near-Term Investable Exposure is Largely Indirect Space mining — encompassing asteroid mining and lunar resource extraction — is transitioning from science fiction to a nascent commercial and policy priority, underpinned by critical mineral scarcity on Earth, falling launch costs, and accelerating lunar infrastructure investment 26 . In the near-term, water extraction from lunar ice or near-Earth asteroids is the most immediate economic driver. Water may potentially be split into liquid hydrogen and oxygen to create rocket propellant, effectively establishing "gas stations" in space 27 . This emerging ecosystem is closely tied to broader government-led initiatives , which continue to anchor early-stage demand for lunar infrastructure and resource development. For example, Firefly Aerospace was awarded a $75 million subcontract by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory to deliver four drones to the Moon’s south pole in support of the MoonFall mission, targeted for no earlier than 2028 28 . From a functional perspective, mining lunar or near-Earth resources enables space agencies to build habitats and refuel spacecraft using locally sourced materials , reducing reliance on transporting inputs from Earth’s deep gravity well. Technological development remains a critical enabling factor. Given communication delays and the hazardous nature of extraterrestrial environments, mining operations will rely heavily on fully autonomous AI systems and advanced robotics . The strategic case for space mining is increasingly reinforced by terrestrial supply chain constraints. AI infrastructure relies on minerals like copper, lithium, and rare earths — resource-rich countries are increasingly imposing extraction taxes and supply controls, creating fiscal and geopolitical pressure across the AI supply chain and reinforcing the strategic case for alternative sourcing 29 . Commercial asteroid mining at scale remains a decade or more away — near-term investable exposure is largely indirect, through launch providers, rover manufacturers, and lunar infrastructure contractors 30 . Two Pillars of Space Mining: Asteroid Mining and Lunar Resource Extraction Space-Based Infrastructure: Transitioning to a Commercially-Driven Data-Focused Sector Space-based infrastructure — encompassing satellite constellations, orbital data centers, space-based power grids, in-orbit manufacturing, and spaceport facilities — is transitioning from a government-led domain to a commercially driven, data-focused sector, with private investment increasingly influencing its growth trajectory 31 . Technology firms are exploring orbital data infrastructure, while aerospace companies are scaling manufacturing capacity to support higher launch cadence and payload complexity. U.S. lawmakers are weighing legislation to boost the data center energy buildout, with space-based power cited as a potential long-term solution to the energy intensity of AI compute — underscoring the convergence of the AI infrastructure and space infrastructure investment themes 32 . At the same time, defense-related infrastructure remains a key anchor of near-term demand. Beyond defense, policymakers are increasingly linking space infrastructure to broader industrial and technological competitiveness. A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers introduced a bill in May 2026 to make property and infrastructure for space-based semiconductor manufacturing explicitly eligible for an investment tax credit — framing space manufacturing competitiveness as a national security issue vis-à-vis China 33 . Ultimately, space-based infrastructure is evolving from a government-funded capability into a commercially scalable platform, but its long-term investment profile will depend on the successful resolution of key economic and technical bottlenecks. Six Elements of Space-Based Infrastructure Conclusion The space economy reflects a classic infrastructure-led innovation cycle , characterized by significant upfront capital investment, uneven monetization timelines, and evolving competitive dynamics. While advancements in launch technology and satellite deployment have materially reduced the cost of accessing space, the next phase of value creation is increasingly dependent on the ability to monetize data, scale services, and establish sustainable commercial models . Space X’s addition to the Nasdaq-100 marked a significant milestone for the space economy’s representation within the index and highlights its growing relevance as a long-term thematic driver. SpaceX represents notable weight in the Nasdaq-100, providing the index with increased exposure to developments in the space economy. Through its exposure to companies involved in cloud computing, AI, semiconductors and satellite-enabled services, the Nasdaq-100 gives investors meaningful exposure to the space economy’s long term growth opportunities. In this context, investment opportunities are likely to diverge across the value chain. Near-term visibility remains strongest in infrastructure and data-driven segments , where demand is supported by defense spending, connectivity needs, and AI integration. By contrast, areas such as space mining, human spaceflight, and in-orbit manufacturing remain long-duration opportunities , with commercialization contingent on technological breakthroughs, regulatory clarity, and continued capital support. As a result, the opportunity is best viewed through a multi-decade lens , where value creation will depend on identifying the segments and business models most likely to translate technological title: Cybersecurity's Next Phase: Competing Business Models in a Growing Market
author: Ilaria Sangalli
description:

While the Nasdaq-100® (NDX®) and the S&P Technology Select Sector Index declined 6.6% and 8.0%, respectively, broader equity markets proved more resilient, with the MSCI World Index gaining 0.5% and the S&P 500 ending the month roughly flat. Against this backdrop, the ISE Cyber Security UCITS™ Index (HUR™) declined 1.8% during the month, demonstrating relative resilience compared with broader technology benchmarks. 

The relative resilience of cybersecurity stocks suggests investors continue to view security spending as a strategic priority rather than a discretionary expense. Importantly, AI adoption appears to be creating additional demand for cybersecurity solutions rather than displacing existing security budgets, as organizations seek to protect AI models, sensitive data and increasingly complex digital environments. content: July highlighted the growing divergence within the technology sector. While the Nasdaq-100® (NDX®) and the S&P Technology Select Sector Index declined 6.6% and 8.0%, respectively, broader equity markets proved more resilient, with the MSCI World Index gaining 0.5% and the S&P 500 ending the month roughly flat. Against this backdrop, the Nasdaq CTA Cybersecurity Index™ Index (NQCYBR™) gained 2.18% during the month, demonstrating relative resilience compared with broader technology benchmarks. 1 The relative resilience of cybersecurity stocks may indicate continued market confidence in security spending, while recent IBM commentary suggests enterprise customers continue to prioritize cybersecurity spending alongside AI investments. 2 Importantly, AI adoption appears to be creating additional demand for cybersecurity solutions rather than displacing existing security budgets, as organizations seek to protect AI models, sensitive data and increasingly complex digital environments. As a result, cybersecurity appears to be a key beneficiary of the broader AI investment cycle. Cybersecurity’s Competitive Landscape: Platforms, Infrastructure and Specialists While the demand outlook for cybersecurity remains robust, competitive dynamics across the industry continue to evolve. The market is no longer defined only by specialist cybersecurity vendors competing against one another. Increasingly, cybersecurity is being embedded into the broader cloud, networking, software and infrastructure platforms that enterprises already use. This evolving landscape is particularly relevant for the NQCYBR Index, which provides exposure to a broad range of companies participating across the cybersecurity ecosystem. Importantly, NQCYBR is not limited to a single cybersecurity business model. The index includes: established cybersecurity vendors such as CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet; technology and infrastructure providers with meaningful cybersecurity businesses, including Cisco, Broadcom, Akamai and Cloudflare; more specialized cybersecurity companies such as Okta, Rubrik, and Qualys. This diversified exposure provides a useful lens through which to examine how the cybersecurity industry is evolving and where value creation is occurring across the ecosystem. Historically, enterprises purchased cybersecurity solutions from specialist vendors focused on specific areas such as endpoint protection, firewalls, identity management, vulnerability management, data protection and threat detection. These companies built their competitive advantage on dedicated security expertise, threat intelligence and rapid product innovation. That remains an important part of the market today, but the competitive landscape is evolving. Cybersecurity is increasingly moving from a collection of standalone point solutions toward broader platforms that aim to protect multiple layers of the enterprise technology stack. Several factors are driving this shift. As cyber threats become more sophisticated and enterprise IT environments grow increasingly complex, organizations are seeking to reduce operational complexity, consolidate vendors and improve visibility across their security environments. This has led to growing demand for integrated platforms that combine multiple security capabilities within a single ecosystem. While best-of-breed solutions continue to play an important role in many security architectures, the broader industry trend has been toward platform consolidation. Among the largest pure-play cybersecurity companies, this is increasingly reflected in product strategies that extend well beyond their original areas of specialization. 3 CrowdStrike has evolved from an endpoint security provider into a broader cybersecurity platform company, expanding its offerings across identity security, cloud security, next-generation SIEM, exposure management, threat intelligence and security operations. 4 In its most recent quarter, reported in June 2026, CrowdStrike generated $5.5 billion in annual recurring revenue, up 24% year over year, while record net new ARR reflected continued customer adoption of the Falcon platform. Momentum was particularly evident in Falcon Flex, CrowdStrike's flexible platform subscription model, with more than 300 accounts added during the quarter. Customers using Falcon Flex collectively represented over $1.9 billion in ending ARR, an increase of 99% year over year, reflecting increasing demand for integrated security platforms that can address multiple cybersecurity needs within a single ecosystem. 5 Palo Alto Networks has also been executing its own platformization strategy, encouraging customers to consolidate security spending across its network security, cloud security and security operations platforms. In its most recent reported quarter 6 , the company reported $8.13 billion in Next-Generation Security (NGS) ARR, representing 60% ARR growth, while management highlighted continued momentum in platformization. The company added approximately 110 net new platformization customers during the quarter, bringing the total to roughly 2,280. These customers represent deeper architectural commitments rather than individual product purchases and have historically exhibited stronger retention and expansion rates. Management also noted that the growing adoption of AI is increasing cybersecurity requirements across enterprise environments, reinforcing demand for integrated security platforms that can provide broader visibility and operational simplicity. 7 Fortinet is pursuing a similar platform-centric strategy, built around its FortiOS operating system, which enables customers to deploy networking and security capabilities across on-premises, cloud and hybrid environments through a unified architecture. This momentum was reflected in the company's Q1 results, with total billings increasing 31% to $2.09 billion, driven by broad-based strength across Secure Networking and Unified SASE. 8 At the same time, infrastructure and networking providers are increasingly embedding cybersecurity into broader enterprise platforms. Cisco has evolved beyond its networking heritage into a broader security platform provider. The company now offers solutions spanning secure access, XDR, AI security and zero-trust architecture, while recent initiatives focused on securing AI infrastructure and AI agents highlight how networking and cybersecurity are becoming increasingly interconnected. Cisco's strategy reflects a growing industry focus on integrating security capabilities directly into enterprise infrastructure and network architectures. An example of this approach is Cisco's Secure AI Factory with Nvidia, which aims to embed security across AI infrastructure deployments. 9 Broadcom participates in cybersecurity through the Symantec enterprise security portfolio, which provides endpoint, network, information and email security solutions across on-premises, cloud and hybrid environments. 10 Akamai illustrates how infrastructure providers are embedding cybersecurity into broader enterprise platforms. While the company built its business around content delivery and edge infrastructure, it has expanded into security through offerings such as web application protection, zero-trust access and microsegmentation. The launch of the Akamai Guardicore Platform further reflects the company's strategy of bringing multiple security functions together within a broader infrastructure platform. 11 However, the cybersecurity industry should not be viewed solely as a competition between large security platforms and infrastructure-led providers. A third group remains highly relevant: specialized cybersecurity vendors focused on specific, mission-critical security functions. These companies may not offer the broadest platforms, but they can remain strategically important where enterprises require deep domain expertise. Examples within NQCYBR include Okta in identity security, Rubrik in cyber resilience and recovery, and Qualys in vulnerability and risk management. Okta, for example, continues to position itself as an independent identity provider, with Q1 revenue of $765 million, up 11% year over year, and remaining performance obligations (RPO) of $4.719 billion, up 16% year over year. Management highlighted that AI agents are creating a new wave of identities that need to be secured and governed alongside human users. 12 Rubrik provides another example of a specialist vendor benefiting from a distinct cybersecurity need: cyber resilience. As ransomware and data breaches increase the importance of recovery, backup and business continuity, Rubrik has positioned itself around helping enterprises recover from cyber incidents. In its latest quarterly results, the company reported subscription ARR of $1.57 billion, up 32% year over year, while total revenue increased 39% year over year to $387.1 million. Management highlighted growing demand for cyber resilience across data, identity, and AI environments, describing Rubrik as an increasingly strategic platform for ‘agentic cyber resilience’. 13 Qualys, meanwhile, remains focused on vulnerability management, compliance and pre-breach risk management. In Q1, Qualys reported revenue of $175.6 million, up 10% year over year, with GAAP operating margin of 35% and non-GAAP operating margin of 46%.  The company's profitability highlights how specialist providers can continue to create value in areas where customers prioritize deep expertise and established workflows, despite ongoing industry consolidation. 14 Source: FactSet. Price Performance as of July 31, 2026 Recent performance trends across NQCYBR constituents reinforce the view that cybersecurity is unlikely to evolve into a simple winner-takes-all market. Performance leadership has not been concentrated in any single business model. Broad cybersecurity platforms such as Fortinet, Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike have delivered strong gains, reflecting continued demand for integrated security offerings. At the same time, specialist providers such as Okta, as well as infrastructure and software companies including Fastly, Datadog and F5, have also ranked among the stronger performers. By contrast, returns have been more mixed for other constituents, including Check Point, OpenText and Zscaler. Taken together, these performance patterns suggest that value creation is occurring across multiple areas of the cybersecurity market. While platformization remains an important trend, enterprise spending continues to support a diverse set of business models, including integrated security platforms, infrastructure-led providers and specialist vendors. For market participants evaluating cybersecurity index exposure, this diversification may be relevant. The index provides exposure across these segments, rather than making a narrow bet on a single approach to cybersecurity. title: Institutional Investing 101: Who the Players Are and How Capital Really Moves
author: Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms
description: Learn what institutional investing is, how capital moves from asset owners to asset managers, and why fiduciary duty, governance, and manager selection shape institutional investment decisions.
content: Key Takeaways Institutional investors collectively manage trillions in global assets on behalf of beneficiaries ranging from individual retirees to entire national populations. The institutional ecosystem operates through two distinct roles: asset owners, who hold capital and set investment mandates, and asset managers, who execute strategies on their behalf. Many institutional investment decision are governed by fiduciary duty, which may include a legal obligation to act solely in the best interests of beneficiaries. Unlike retail investors, institutional investors usually operate on multi-decade or perpetual time horizons to meet obligations decades in the future. Capital allocation decisions pass through investment committees, boards, and often external consultants before reaching markets, a structure designed to protect beneficiaries. Manager selection involves rigorous quantitative and qualitative analysis, and the relationship continues through ongoing performance monitoring, compliance review, and periodic re-evaluation. Institutional investors represent more than US$70 trillion in investable assets globally , giving them significant influence over capital markets. Despite this scale, many professionals entering the space don’t fully understand how institutional capital moves, who makes the decisions, what governs them, and why the process looks so different from retail investing. Whether working in asset management, market infrastructure, or product marketing, professionals in these roles need a clear mental map of the institutional ecosystem. Otherwise, the terminology may become confusing, timelines may see arbitrary, and governance structures can be hard to understand. Understanding the institutional ecosystem requires knowing the key players, from pension funds and sovereign wealth funds to the asset managers they appoint and the consultants who advise them. It also calls for knowing how capital flows through the system, what governs the decisions at each stage, and what makes institutional investing so different from the retail context most professionals understand. What Is Institutional Investing? Institutional investing refers to the management of large pools of capital by organizations on behalf of beneficiaries or stakeholders. These organizations pool capital and invest at volumes that individual investors cannot access. There are several types of institutional investors in the landscape. Pension funds invest retirement assets on behalf of plan participants, and university and charitable endowments invest to fund ongoing operations and perpetual missions. Insurance companies invest policyholders' premium income to meet future claims, while sovereign wealth funds manage national reserves on behalf of entire populations. In each case, the capital belongs to someone else. The point of distinction in its institutional world (managing money for others) defines the principle of fiduciary duty , which means the institution is legally obligated to act solely in the beneficiaries' interests. Understanding the Institutional Difference For professionals new to this space, the institutional world can at first seem confusing, with mandates, governance structures, and an environment different from retail investing. However, the layers of governance are designed to protect beneficiaries, and understanding this is the foundation for everything else in the institutional ecosystem. Who Are the Key Players in Institutional Investing? There are several player types in the institutional landscape , each with its own source of capital, set of beneficiaries, and investment objective. Asset Owners: The Capital Holders Asset owners are the institutions that hold capital for others and are responsible for how it is invested. There are four main types: Pension Funds manage retirement assets on behalf of plan participants, investing to meet future benefit obligations. They operate across two structures: defined benefit plans and defined contribution plans. Endowments and Foundations manage capital for universities, hospitals, and charitable organizations Sovereign Wealth Funds are state-owned investment vehicles managing national reserves, often with decades-long investment horizons set up to preserve resource wealth for future generations. Insurance Companies invest premium income to meet future policyholder claims with a strategy shaped by the duration of liabilities. Asset Managers: The Investment Executors Asset managers are the firms hired by asset owners to execute investment strategies on their behalf. They range from large, diversified global managers to specialized boutiques focused on a single asset class or strategy. They are selected through competitive due diligence processes that evaluate the investment process, team, risk management, and alignment with mandate requirements. How Capital Flows Through the Institutional Investment System Institutional capital flows through a structured chain of governance, documentation, and oversight designed to protect beneficiaries at every stage. Understanding this chain can help explain how decisions are made and why they take time. The Decision Chain The process usually starts with a formal Investment Policy Statement , which defines objectives, risk parameters, asset allocation ranges, and performance benchmarks. After the policy is set, the asset owner issues mandates to asset managers: formal agreements that specify investment guidelines, benchmarks, fee structures, and reporting requirements. Asset managers then execute strategies within those mandate parameters and report performance back to the asset owner. Custodians and administrators handle settlement, safekeeping, and independent accounting, which adds another layer of verification at the point of execution. The Role of Investment Consultants Most asset owners use a consultant in this process. The consultant acts as an intermediary with an advisory capacity with advice on asset allocation, manager selection, portfolio construction, and performance monitoring. More than 85% of US institutional asset owners use investment consultants for help with manager selection, performance monitoring, and asset allocation. This layered structure explains why institutional capital often moves deliberately, as each decision passes through multiple checkpoints before reaching markets. What Makes Institutional Investing Different from Retail Investing? While retail investing and institutional investing operate in the same markets, they have different rules of scale, time, and accountability. Scale and Time Horizon Institutional portfolios aren’t construed to serve a single individual but thousands or millions of beneficiaries. As a result, investment decisions operate on a different scale, with large asset size, long-term investment horizons, regulatory constraints, and a governance framework.  Many institutions also operate on time horizons ranging from 30 years for pension funds to perpetuity for endowments. Governance and Fiduciary Duty Where a retail investor makes personal decisions about their own capital, institutional decisions are governed by formal structures and a legal obligation to others. The institutions have a fiduciary duty to act solely in the beneficiaries' best interests it shapes every decision, from asset allocation to manager selection. Decisions are driven by investment committees, and evaluating an investment manager is a complex and detailed process of operational due diligence , governance assessment, and compliance review, often conducted over several months. Institutional investors also face regulatory and stakeholder reporting obligations to regulators, boards, and beneficiaries that have no equivalent in retail contexts. These differences mean that professionals supporting institutional clients must understand longer timelines, formal processes, and the weight of fiduciary responsibility. As a result, investment decisions operate on a different scale, with large asset size, long-term investment horizons, regulatory constraints, and a governance framework.  Many institutions also operate on time horizons ranging from 30 years for pension funds to perpetuity for endowments. Governance and Fiduciary Duty Where a retail investor makes personal decisions about their own capital, institutional decisions are governed by formal structures and a legal obligation to others. The institutions have a fiduciary duty to act solely in the beneficiaries' best interests it shapes every decision, from asset allocation to manager selection. Decisions are driven by investment committees, and evaluating an investment manager is a complex and detailed process of operational due diligence , governance assessment, and compliance review, often conducted over several months. Institutional investors also face regulatory and stakeholder reporting obligations to regulators, boards, and beneficiaries that have no equivalent in retail contexts. These differences mean that professionals supporting institutional clients must understand longer timelines, formal processes, and the weight of fiduciary responsibility. How Asset Managers Are Selected and Monitored Selecting an asset manager is a critical decision for an institutional investor, and it is typically governed by process, documentation, and fiduciary accountability. How Managers Are Selected Asset owners conduct structured searches to identify managers suited to the mandates. The manager search and selection process usually has three components: the pool of managers, an analysis of their track records, and a quantitative analysis of the investment process. The quantitative review covers their performance history, risk metrics, and return attribution, while the qualitative assessment evaluates the investment team's process consistency, organizational culture, and operational infrastructure. Ongoing Monitoring and Reporting Oversight tends to continues even after a manager is selected. This includes a periodic review of the investment strategy to ensure the manager continues to execute as expected. Monitoring covers adherence to strategy, compliance with mandate parameters, and early detection of process drift. Underperformance or material changes to the investment team or process may result in termination. Data quality and transparency are foundational throughout the process, and asset owners depend on accurate, timely reporting to fulfill their fiduciary obligations to beneficiaries. How Nasdaq Supports Institutional Investment Decisions For investment teams navigating manager due diligence, portfolio monitoring, and ongoing performance analysis, data and manual processes may create a burden. This may make it harder to move at the speed and with the confidence that fiduciary responsibility demands. Nasdaq eVestment™ is an institutional investment data and analytics platform that connects asset managers, consultants, and asset owners through a centralized ecosystem.  For asset owners conducting manager searches, it offers access to standardized performance data, peer comparisons, and qualitative manager profiles. Nasdaq eVestment™ also offers monitoring teams a platform with independent data across the firm, personnel, and portfolio risk, to address transparency needs. Institutional Investment FAQs What is institutional investing? Institutional investing refers to the management of large pools of capital by organizations, such as pension funds, endowments, insurance companies, and sovereign wealth funds, on behalf of beneficiaries or stakeholders. What is the difference between an asset owner and an asset manager? Asset owners are institutions that hold capital on behalf of others and set the investment strategy. Asset managers are firms hired by asset owners to execute investment strategies in accordance with specific mandates. What is fiduciary duty in institutional investing? Fiduciary duty is the legal obligation to act solely in the best interests of beneficiaries when making investment decisions. How do institutional investors select asset managers? Asset owners tend to conduct structured manager searches, often with support from investment consultants, to identify managers suited to a specific mandate. Due diligence involves both quantitative analysis and qualitative assessment of the investment team, process consistency, and organizational culture. The process typically extends over several months before a final selection is made. Why do institutional investment decisions take so long? Institutional investment decisions pass through multiple governance layers before capital is committed. Each stage involves formal review, documentation, and compliance checks to protect beneficiaries' interests. What is an investment mandate? An investment mandate is a formal agreement between an asset owner and an asset manager that specifies investment guidelines, benchmarks, fee structures, and reporting requirements. It defines the parameters within which the asset manager must operate. What is AUM? AUM stands for Assets Under Management, the total market value of assets that an investment manager oversees on behalf of clients at a given point in time. © 2026 Nasdaq, Inc. title: Nasdaq-100® Inside the Index: Starbucks (SBUX)
author: Nasdaq Index Insights Team
description: In this edition of Inside the Index, we examine Starbucks (SBUX), one of the world's largest coffeehouse chains, and explore how its company-operated store model and ongoing turnaround efforts are helping drive renewed sales and profit growth.
content: VOL 1 • ISSUE 08 • AUGUST 2026 Starbucks runs most of its stores itself. So when it reinvents the experience, the upside lands on its own books. SBUX • Consumer Discretionary • Index Constituent This Issue — SBUX Starbucks, a current Nasdaq-100® constituent at ~0.55% index weight, is one of the world's largest coffeehouse networks, and it operates most of its stores itself rather than franchising. The "Back to Starbucks" turnaround under CEO Brian Niccol has now delivered four straight quarters of positive global comparable sales, and Q3 FY2026 results beat consensus on revenue, margin and profit by a wide margin, prompting a raised full-year outlook. Key Figures Business Model & Revenue Drivers A Coffeehouse It Mostly Runs Itself Cafes that Starbucks owns and staffs generate 82.7% of revenue ($30.7B in FY2025), far more than the franchise-heavy model common in fast food; licensed stores and Channel Development (CPG, foodservice, the Nestlé alliance) make up the rest. Because Starbucks owns those stores, every improvement it makes (faster service, new drinks, a better app) lands on its own books rather than a franchisee's. As traffic returns, the full store margin returns with it. Competitive Moat Why the Brand Is Hard to Replicate The harder thing to copy is the habit Starbucks created: premium coffee as a daily ritual. Beverages are 60.5% of revenue in the latest filings, customized drinks bought several times a week at prices plain coffee could not command. Scale reinforces it over time. Starbucks Rewards ties the habit to an app that remembers the order and the payment, keeping the brand a tap away. Operating Strengths Three Structural Advantages 1. 35.8M U.S. 90-day active Rewards members. Loyalty engagement keeps climbing, reinforcing the daily ritual behind repeat visits and app orders. 2. 22,993 international stores. More stores now operate outside North America than inside it, evidence the cafe format travels. 3. $27.4B North America revenue. The home market supplies 73.5% of revenue, funding renovations and overseas growth. Growth Catalysts What Grows the Business Next The turnaround is no longer early-innings. Q3 FY2026 (ended June 28) marked the fourth straight quarter of positive global comparable sales, up 7.9% on both traffic (+4.2%) and ticket (+3.5%), beating consensus on revenue, adjusted EPS, and margin by wide margins. Adjusted operating margin expanded 430 bps year over year to 14.4%, the second straight quarter of margin gains. Management raised full-year guidance across the board: adjusted EPS to $2.55–$2.65, U.S. comp sales to at least 6%, and operating margin to above 11%. The $2B cost-savings plan is tracking on schedule through FY2028, and the company repaid $1.8B of debt in the quarter alone. • Menu innovation. Refreshers posted double-digit U.S. growth and food attach rates improved; the pipeline includes new Frappuccino platforms into Q4. • Store uplifts. The company is on track for at least 1,500 coffeehouse renovations by fiscal year-end, with revamped stores showing faster transaction growth. • Asset-light international. Converting China to a licensed joint venture with Boyu Capital lowers future capital needs and should improve returns on invested capital. Historical Context Revenue Kept Climbing Through the Reset Valuation & Investment Thesis What the Multiple Is Pricing Starbucks trades near 35× forward earnings, or ~33× on FY2027 consensus ($3.17 EPS) — a premium to franchised peers like McDonald's (20×) and Yum! (22×). The stock has run from a $78.46 trough last October to $105.12, up 34%, and 18 of 40 covering analysts rate it Buy with a consensus target of $110.62. The premium increasingly prices margin recovery already arriving, not just hoped for: adjusted operating margin has expanded for two straight quarters toward its historical mid-teens range. Key Risks What Could Change the Story • Durability of traffic, since some of the 4.2% U.S. transaction growth reflects easy comparisons against a weak prior year rather than structural gains. • China opacity, now that the retail business has been deconsolidated into a licensed joint venture with Boyu Capital; only equity earnings ($53M in Q3) are disclosed for the second-largest Starbucks market (8,011 stores). • Commodity costs, with coffee prices still a margin swing factor even as recent tariff refunds provided a tailwind. • Leverage, with net debt of $18.8B and negative book equity still limiting financial flexibility, despite $1.8B of debt repaid this quarter. • Consumer spending and competition, where a discretionary slowdown or share loss to Dutch Bros, CAVA, and independent cafes could slow traffic. What This Means For You The Index Angle, in Plain Terms In Your Index Fund — If you hold a fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index®, you already own this. • Index composition follows transparent eligibility criteria, and SBUX is a current constituent at ~0.55% index weight: about 55 cents of every $100 tracking the index sits in Starbucks. • It's the cup you already buy on the way to work, and the loyalty app that remembers your order. • Because Starbucks runs most of its own stores, your fund feels the company's full swing in profit, the strong years and the slow ones. Decoding the Jargon Two terms doing the heavy lifting in this issue. • Comparable store sales (comps). Sales growth from stores open at least a year, which strips out new openings. Rising comps come from existing cafes selling more, rather than from new store openings. • Operating margin. The share of revenue left after the cost of running the stores. It fell to 7.8% in FY2025, and has since expanded to 14.4% (adjusted) in Q3 FY2026, evidence the recovery is arriving faster than expected. Bottom Line If you own a Nasdaq-100® fund, you already own Starbucks, and its rebound is no longer just a plan. Sales and profits are growing again, the kind of result the turnaround was built to deliver. The Inside the Index series profiles one constituent each issue, from software to soft drinks and computer chips to potato chips, exploring what makes each business distinctive and the metrics investors should know. title: Nasdaq-100® Outperforms the S&P 500 on Earnings Growth and Surprise Trends
author: Salvatore Bruno, CETF®
description: Explore how the Nasdaq-100® has outperformed the S&P 500 in revenue growth, EPS growth, and earnings surprise trends from Q1 2023 to Q1 2026.
content: Key takeaways Nasdaq-100 has delivered stronger top-line growth than the S&P 500 over the last three years, with year-over-year quarterly revenue growth reaching 18.6% in Q1 2026 versus 11.8% for the S&P 500. Nasdaq-100 dominated EPS growth in almost all quarters with historically strong EPS growth of 45.6% in Q1 2026 vs 28.8% for the S&P 500, with robust earnings contribution from its largest constituents. Nasdaq-100’s growth leadership is broad-based across sectors, with notable revenue and EPS strength in Technology , Consumer Discretionary , Energy and Basic Materials . On surprise trends, Nasdaq-100 remains stronger on an index-weighted basis, and excluding Nasdaq-100 constituents materially weakens the broader S&P 500’s revenue and EPS beat profile. Nasdaq-100 continues to lead on revenue growth and, in several periods, EPS growth The Nasdaq-100 (NDX®) has outperformed the S&P 500 (SPX) on year-over-year growth in quarterly revenue over the last three years with revenue growth rising from 4.5% in Q1’23 to 18.6% in Q1’26, versus 4.2% to 11.8% for the S&P 500. The outperformance has been consistently maintained from Q2’23 to date. EPS growth has been more volatile quarter to quarter, but the Nasdaq-100 still delivered higher growth rates than the S&P 500 in 12 consecutive quarters, with the last quarter of underperformance recorded in Q1’23. In Q2’23, Nasdaq-100 delivered strong EPS growth of 17.3% while the S&P 500 recorded a negative growth of -2.5%. It was the first of seven instances during which NDX outperformed on EPS growth by at least 10 percentage points, including 29 percentage points of outperformance in Q4’23. Sector growth rates showcase broad-based Nasdaq-100 leadership The revenue growth by sector (per ICB Industry) shows Nasdaq-100 leadership across most sectors, with outperformance in major sectors such as Technology (15.2% vs. 13.0%), Consumer Discretionary (10.0% vs 5.8%), Basic Materials (3.7% vs -1.9%), Real Estate (12.4% vs. 7.3%), and Energy (12.9% vs. -3.8%). The S&P 500 leads only in a limited number of areas such as Consumer Staples (6.2% vs. 4.3%). In other sectors, there were similar growth rates, though the Nasdaq-100 has no exposure to Financials by design (see Table 1). The EPS growth story also supports the sector dominance of NDX with notable outperformance in Consumer Discretionary, Health Care, Basic Materials and Energy as shown in Table 2. Nasdaq-100 generally outperformed on an index-weighted basis in revenue and earnings beat performance based on FactSet data Based on the absolute number of companies that beat consensus estimates, NDX looks like a slight underperformer (on average, 83% of companies beat EPS estimates per quarter vs 87% for SPX) (see Chart 3). When it comes to index weight, NDX significantly outperformed, with 86% on average beating EPS expectations compared to just 63% for SPX.  That is, on average, 23 percentage points of outperformance per quarter during the last three years. Furthermore, SPX’s EPS beat performance drastically declined from Q2 2025 onwards while NDX was relatively resilient during the period (see Chart 4). When it comes to revenue beating market expectations, Nasdaq-100 has outperformed S&P 500 in every quarter for the last three years (see Chart 5). On average, 83% of NDX’s index weight beat revenue expectations each quarter compared to 77% for SPX. Based on absolute number of companies, 78% of NDX constituents beat revenue estimates compared to 68% for SPX (see Chart 6). Excluding Nasdaq-100 constituents weakens the broader S&P 500 profile 87 out of the 100 companies in NDX are also in SPX, representing about 51% of the market capitalization of SPX (as of March 31, 2026).  This overlap has greatly helped drive SPX fundamental results in recent years. When we consider SPX excluding NDX constituents, the S&P 500’s beat profile deteriorates meaningfully. Without Nasdaq-100 members, the S&P 500’s average revenue beat rate falls from 77% to 70% (see Chart 7), while the average EPS beat rate declines from 63% to 47% (see Chart 8). This suggests that Nasdaq-100 companies account for a disproportionate share of earnings and revenue surprise strength within the broader U.S. large-cap universe. Overall, the Nasdaq-100 has been the stronger index not only on aggregate revenue and EPS growth, but also on the breadth of reported results. Even where the S&P 500 shows a slightly higher share of companies beating EPS expectations, the Nasdaq-100 remains decisively stronger on an index-weighted basis, indicating that its larger constituents have contributed more meaningfully to index-level outperformance.
